# Empty Group Input Compatibility Proposal

This proposal remains under the old entry point because early discussions and investigations will find it through the terms Empty component group record and Configured input-length compatibility. Do not treat the initial direction as the current interface specification: it records the approach that was intended at the time to handle two kinds of behavior with one relatively small change.

The original wording was straightforward: an empty component group has no readable content, so it need not occupy a position in the result; when the configured input length does not match the content, continue with the processable portion. These two statements were put together not because a shared implementation had been verified, but because the goal was to reduce branching at the pattern execution entry point. The rollback criteria listed at the time were also narrow: they asked only whether any caller depended on an empty position or whether repeated processing produced different results. That judgment later proved insufficient, but it is retained below so the context referenced by old links can be checked.

By the second revision, the interface review had already taken place. The record for AURL-207 is interface_reviewed; the card requires using existing tests or examples to trigger Empty component group record and writing the user paths not yet covered back into the card. That record only shows that this went through interface review; it cannot replace a decision about the result representation. The earlier draft turned "can't see the content" into "no need to record it"; that is exactly where the observation and the decision were conflated.

The patch-like idea not adopted at the time was: always retain one position internally while continuing to omit the empty position externally. It appeared able to leave existing results unchanged while preserving more state in the implementation, but the problem did not go away: callers still could not determine from the public result whether the empty component had participated in matching. Another idea was to expose the empty position directly; this would change the result shape, but the old draft did not identify an adopter and did not provide enough material to assess the change. Neither approach should be endorsed on the basis of "input length compatibility."

Accordingly, the v1 default direction was corrected to the weaker historical assessment: whether empty records are retained must be discussed independently of length configuration. No new final representation rule is given here. The old proposal's "can be omitted if there is no content" portion is outdated and should no longer be cited as an interface decision; it remains in this document because some old investigations only documented this layer.

The material on the length issue is also limited. The check proposed by AURL-224 is to run the initial processing and the reprocessing separately for Configured input-length compatibility and record whether the content or diagnostics are stable. It does not state that a length mismatch should be truncated, padded, or rejected, nor does it specify the correct result form for an empty group. The earlier wording that made "continue with the processable portion" the default handling was an unconfirmed extrapolation. It can only be treated as a candidate again: if the initial processing and reprocessing differ, first isolate length handling, then determine whether the difference comes from content, length configuration, or diagnostics; do not patch the group representation and then declare compatibility.

The comparison table retained here is not a release commitment:

| Candidate | Rationale in the old proposal | Outstanding determination |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Produce no record | Shorter result; existing callers see no extra position | Whether missing and empty records need to be distinguished |
| Produce an empty position | Calls to Fang Ke see the component position | Whether the change in result shape is acceptable |
| Retain internally, omit externally | Attempts to retain both state and the old result | Whether the public interface consequently loses necessary information |

include/ada/url_pattern.h continues to serve as a reference point for the pattern interface declaration. It is useful for checking the name and nearby declarations, but it is insufficient as a substitute for this old proposal when determining execution results. If someone later fills in a specific user path via AURL-207, they should map that path to the "whether missing and empty records need to be distinguished" issue in the table above; if they obtain records of the initial and repeated processing via AURL-224, they should first determine whether it concerns length only, and then decide whether to reopen the choice of group representation.

This page covers a topic adjacent to DOC-20, but Unicode hostname canonicalization and Unicode search-parameter ordering should not be used to infer the results for empty groups or lengths. There are only two unanswered questions at present: whether the public result needs to represent the position of an empty component; whether two processing passes with the configured length are stable. The old proposal did not resolve them.

# Unicode Host and Query Troubleshooting Tree

The earliest content left on this page was a very narrowly scoped troubleshooting note: if the state is abnormal after Unicode hostname processing, check `include/ada/ada_idna.h`; if Unicode output cannot be reproduced consistently, rerun it through the existing test entry point. The two symptoms were presented side by side from the start, and the old page did not say whether they were caused by the same entry point or leave an input that could reproduce them consistently.

The path in the old troubleshooting record is `include/ada/ada_idna.h` under revision `v_prev` of `internal/ada-url-runtime`. Originally, the only matching terms listed beside the path were `pattern`, `unicode`, `urlpattern`, `containing`, `utf-8`, `utf`, `com`, and `idna`. This was enough to lead someone to the vicinity of the declarations, but not enough to establish calling relationships; do not infer which implementation this issue belongs to from the directory containing the file.

## Approach Recorded on the Old Page

In practice, the early version was used roughly as follows:

```text
An anomaly occurs
└─ First take the issue name or call name to ada_idna.h
   ├─ Abnormal hostname state → check Unicode hostname canonicalization
   └─ Unstable output order → check Unicode search-parameter ordering
```

This split can still serve as a starting point, but "looked in the file" cannot be treated as "found the caller." The old page therefore keeps the two names in the same tree as a historical record; do not read it as a complete account of the implementation.

## Investigation Timeline

On 2025-09-24, AURL-208 moved from To Do to In Progress. On 2025-09-25, it moved from In Progress to Done. What can be confirmed here is the card's status change, not any fix details or stable results inferred from it. If abnormal hostname state is encountered again now, you should still first verify the actual entry point and version that the card referred to at the time, rather than interpreting Done directly as meaning that the current entry point is still correct.

On 2025-10-22, AURL-225 left sample_attached. By 2025-10-23, assignee_changed had occurred on the card. A sample exists, but this page does not include its contents or enough material to say which units it covers; the query parameter ordering branch can therefore only call for fresh sampling, and must not assume the attachment is a record of a passing regression run.

## Troubleshooting Tree

```text
Symptom: Abnormal state after Unicode hostname processing
└─ A. Preserve the original input, the processed hostname, and the entry point where the anomaly occurs
   ├─ Occurs only after Unicode hostname canonicalization
   │  └─ Verify the caller still using this name, the actual version, the entry point, and the current result
   ├─ A change in query ordering is also observed
   │  └─ Copy the same input and record Unicode search-parameter ordering separately
   └─ Occurs in only one run
      └─ Do not write back "fixed" yet; retain the run's entry point and full output for a second verification

Symptom: Unicode output cannot be reproduced consistently
└─ B. Run the same input through the existing test entry point
   ├─ Output is the same every time
   │  └─ Still retain the affected units and adjacent unchanged units, then compare entry points and versions
   ├─ Output order differs
   │  └─ Classify it under Unicode search-parameter ordering; the hostname branch cannot be used as a substitute
   └─ The same output cannot be obtained
      └─ Save the sample; do not infer that processing has recovered from a single different output
```

### Branch A: Hostname State

The first question is "which caller is still using Unicode hostname canonicalization," not "is this header file the root cause." For the caller, record the actual version, entry point, and current result together. If only the issue name can be found, stop the investigation here; if all that remains is declarations or adjacency information for `include/ada/ada_idna.h`, stop here as well. The old page mixed file matches with relationship verification, and that is precisely the correction that needed to be made later.

Save the input and results separately. Do not collapse the original Unicode hostname, the processed value, the state change, and the value when read again into the single phrase "abnormal state." Only then can you tell whether the anomaly appeared after canonicalization or whether the entry point itself had already changed the result when reading it. There is currently no stable caller sample available to cite, so this section remains a troubleshooting requirement, not a confirmed attribution.

If the reviewer has only a screenshot showing "incorrect after processing," return to the entry point first, and do not immediately change the IDNA rules. You can check whether the version is still the same, whether the same entry point was used, and whether the same input was obtained; if any of these is unclear, mark the result as unverified. On this page, differences caused by different versions and differences caused by different entry points must not be lumped together.

### Branch B: Query Parameter Ordering

Collect samples for Unicode search-parameter ordering separately. The historical activity on AURL-225 only shows that sample_attached was attached later, not that every output in the sample was verified. When rerunning, save both the affected units and adjacent unchanged units; if only one unit changes, you must still record its comparison with the unchanged units, and must not take "the order looks normal" to mean that the entire output path is already stable.

The recovery steps after a failure here are straightforward: when output is unstable on the first attempt, do not keep changing the input and then pick a result that looks normal, and do not use a pass on the hostname branch in place of the ordering branch. Keep multiple outputs for the same input; if it cannot be reproduced, record the test entry point and the version used for the run, and return to "insufficient samples" rather than "the issue has disappeared." If it can be reproduced, record the change only as an ordering observation, without adding a hostname-state conclusion for now.

## File Entry Point and Stopping Points

`include/ada/ada_idna.h` is the local navigation point currently visible. It can help locate declarations and neighboring objects related to `unicode`, `utf-8`, and `idna`; on this page, it does not establish any particular caller, version used for a run, or output result. To continue, trace back from an actual caller, then paste that caller's input, version, and results back into the corresponding branch. Without a caller, do not use a filename, issue name, or keyword match as a substitute.

AURL-208 points to the work records for abnormal Unicode hostname state, and AURL-225 points to the records of unstable Unicode output and samples. The two cards are retained here only as entry points into the investigation; a card's status or the presence of an attachment does not mean this page already has complete evidence. For the related compatibility checks, see DOC-21 separately, but do not copy the conclusions from the other page into this troubleshooting tree.

## Points Still Prone to Misinterpretation

1. `Unicode hostname canonicalization` and `Unicode search-parameter ordering` are two observation names that can be recorded separately. The old page placed them near the same entry point, which does not justify combining them into a single root cause.
2. `Done`, `sample_attached`, and a reproducible output are a status, a sample-related action, and a run observation, respectively. The three are not interchangeable.
3. Finding a declaration, finding a caller, and reproducing output are three stopping points. When you complete the first stopping point, do not casually record the other two as completed.

If the next review can provide only the issue name, it is enough to retain the name and the gaps; if it provides the actual entry point, add the version, input, result, and comparison with adjacent units. Until these items can be matched up within the same branch, this page should still be used as an old troubleshooting record, not as the current authoritative conclusion.

# Port Semantics and IDNA Migration

This page was originally a record of finding a file from an issue name. In retrospect, what actually needs to be migrated is not a directory whose existence has already been confirmed, but the lookup action itself: the old record goes from the name to `include/ada/url_pattern_helpers-inl.h`, while the new record must follow the same clue back to the specified revision, then inspect local declarations, direct references, and caller results. The frozen materials do not provide a replacement file, so this work cannot be written up as though the file move has been completed.

## What the old entry point can still preserve

`include/ada/url_pattern_helpers-inl.h` is still a valid starting point for retrieval. It can bring terms such as `pattern`, `canon`, `space`, and `port` back to a block of adjacent code, and can also help old compatibility-check records find their place again. But path names, helper suffixes, and issue terms cannot by themselves establish implementation ownership. The revision in the record is `v_prev`; lock this version first, then confirm the reference relationships, to avoid filling in the adjacency from another copy of the code.

The old page shows two check tracks side by side, which makes "compatibility" easy to turn into a generic term with no object. After migration, the two names are still retained, but each track separately stores its input, local processing, and caller result. Trailing-space port semantics focuses on trailing spaces in port input; Valid IDNA mapping compatibility focuses on how valid IDNA mappings behave in old calls. Both can belong to the same R2026.09 check, but neither can stand in for the other's result.

```text
Old issue name / call name

include/ada/url_pattern_helpers-inl.h

v_prev: local references for pattern / canon / space / port
        |
        +--> Trailing-space port semantics: raw input -> port-processing observation
        |
        +--> Valid IDNA mapping compatibility: actual call -> caller result
```

The old side of the migration is "an issue name or call name points to a file." The new side is "the file path remains the entry point, but behavioral judgments must return to the direct relationships at the specified revision." Both sides need to be retained: the old side supports historical lookup, and the new side supports this round of verification. The current materials do not contain a second file path, so a seemingly complete old-path-to-new-path mapping cannot be filled in.

Follow the actual operation in the order below; the order itself is the reusable addition to this page.

1. **Preserve the original locator.** Copy the original issue name, call name, and `include/ada/url_pattern_helpers-inl.h`; do not first change the old names into a new umbrella term. The original locator helps revisit the old page, but represents only the search starting point.
2. **Pin the version.** Use the file contents for `v_prev` as the boundary for this local check. First confirm whether what you see is a declaration, a reference, or whether both can be followed to a caller; if you can see only a path, stop at the path level.
3. **Separate the inputs.** For Trailing-space port semantics, preserve whether the input has trailing spaces and where the spaces occur. For Valid IDNA mapping compatibility, preserve the domain-name input being checked and the observation after mapping. Do not add raw strings that the materials do not provide.
4. **Follow the direct relationships.** Continue along the actual references of `pattern`, `canon`, `space`, and `port`; if you can confirm only a local declaration, stop the record at the declaration. If you can confirm a call, add the value or error received by the caller.
5. **Put the result back on the corresponding track.** The port track records only the port-processing observation, and the IDNA track records only the mapping and caller result. File existence, a name match, or the appearance of a call name cannot substitute for a result.

There are therefore two possibilities for "where it moves from and to." If the specified revision still shows the same file as the direct entry point, the migration changes only the verification order, not the file location; only if the actual reference leaves that file should a relationship between the new path and the old path be added. The existing materials confirm only the initial entry layer and provide no result for the latter case.

AURL-209 are cards that can be used to continue navigating this track. Its historical record has a processing window between 2025-09-29 and 2025-10-02. The intervening card note says: "Don't close this one yet; this AURL-209 card still has one unconfirmed item in Trailing-space port semantics." The current frozen materials provide only the object under review and this unconfirmed note, not a specific input, output, or test log, so this version does not write any of these processing outcomes as confirmed facts.

Advancing the card to later nodes does not change this boundary either. If only the input is added later, update only the input; if a local reference is added, connect the reference to the corresponding `space` or `port` relationship; only when the caller result also appears can this check track be changed from a lookup record into a compatibility-result record. Whichever layer is missing, leave the gap at its original location; do not use material from the other track as a substitute.

## The old call for Valid IDNA mapping compatibility

The migration focus of the IDNA track is different. The old record retains the name, but does not provide a caller example that can be copied directly into the page. During verification, still start from `include/ada/url_pattern_helpers-inl.h`, follow the actual references of `v_prev` to confirm the call location, and then record the mapping result observed by the caller once the call is found. When you see only a name or a local declaration, do not interpret "valid" to mean that the mapping has passed.

This track does not explain port behavior, nor does it cover the complete IDNA rule description. It only needs to answer whether the old call actually passed through that local relationship and what result the caller received. DOC-22 are adjacent validation-design records that can be used for continued navigation; the validation arrangement they should preserve is not repeated here. If a new call entry appears in the future, note on this page whether it replaces the old lookup path or only covers one local call under Valid IDNA mapping compatibility.

## Batches and restoring the old path

At present, the only identifiable migration batch has three work entry points: the old issue name and call name find the file; the specified revision is used to check direct references; and, once there is a result, the caller observation is written back to the long-term record. R2026.09 represent only the scope of this compatibility check; they do not mean that a directory switch has already been completed.

If the new verification finds that the path is unchanged, the recovery method is to return to the old entry record, retain the original issue name, call name, and observed findings, and withdraw the unsubstantiated judgment about the new path. If only the verification order changed, what is restored is the record entry point, not the conversion of unconfirmed behavior into the old behavior. If the direct reference has actually moved, retain the old path as the historical entry, add the new path, the corresponding local object, and the known result; without a result, add only a migration clue and do not write it as completed.

Two cases require stopping: there is only a path, with no reference at the specified revision; or there is a local declaration, with no caller result. Both are unfinished items in the migration. The "one item remains unconfirmed" note left by AURL-209 must remain under the port track; it must not be deleted because the processing window has ended, and it must not be summarized as "compatibility confirmed."

## Materials retained now

Retaining `internal/ada-url-runtime`, `v_prev`, and `include/ada/url_pattern_helpers-inl.h`, together with the old issue name and call name, ensures that later searches can still return to the same place. Retaining `pattern`, `canon`, `space`, and `port` distinguishes the local references rather than combining them into a new module-level conclusion. This version adds no files, functions, commands, or outputs. This record preserves two issues discussed side by side during R2026.09: Search and hash delimiter retention, and Empty DNS host rejection. There were two options at the time. One was to treat delimiter retention and empty hosts as a single canon issue and tighten input handling with the same set of changes; the other was to separate the observed behaviors first, record assessments that could be reviewed independently, and then decide whether a shared underlying change was needed. The meeting chose the latter. The reason was simple: for Search, the first question was whether users could preserve the boundaries they had entered; for an empty DNS host, it was whether that host state should be accepted. # Opaque path and host rollback troubleshooting tree

## Record the observations first

Two names to start with on this page: Opaque path space preservation and Full host-setter transaction rollback. Both have been pointed to `include/ada/url.h`, but so far we've only seen adjacent declarations in the existing h module, so don't treat the path itself as the implementation location.

The observations so far are limited: for the same kind of URL input, one call preserved the spaces in the opaque path, while another call had a different visible result; another question, still unverified, is whether the original URL state was fully retained after the host setter failed. Don't combine the two into a single parser issue yet.

## Diagnostic branches

```text
Difference observed
├─ pathname / href differences occur only in the opaque path
│  ├─ First save the raw inputs for the successful and failed calls
│  ├─ Compare pathname, then href
│  └─ Don't start by using normal path rules to explain it
└─ host setter returns failure or the result is unexpected
   ├─ Record scheme, host, port, and pathname before the call
   ├─ Record the same set of visible fields after the failure
   └─ First check whether the old values are still there, then discuss rollback
```

If both branches occur, save the two results separately. Don't write them up as the same conversion just because they both pass through a URL object.

## Where to check now

Use the issue names and call names to navigate to `include/ada/url.h`, and first check the immediate neighbors of the declarations related to URL, parser, opaque path, and setter. This is useful for checking public entry points and field names, but isn't enough on its own to establish the actual call order. The raw inputs, visible fields before and after the call, and failure return values need to be saved separately.

To confirm:

- whether spaces in the opaque path are preserved before parsing or restored during pathname / href output;
- whether all modified fields return together to their pre-call state when the host setter fails;
- whether the two differences occur only in the current version.

Stop at these questions for now; there's no need to fill in unseen implementation details to reach a conclusion.

# Opaque path and host rollback troubleshooting tree

## Separate the two issues at the outset

This record initially placed two names side by side: Opaque path space preservation, Full host-setter transaction rollback. Both can be traced back from around the local declarations in `include/ada/url.h`, but the diagnostic paths differ in practice. The former checks whether spaces in an opaque path change between input, parsing and visible output; the latter checks whether the URL object is left partially modified after a host setter fails.

When you encounter anomalous behavior in R2026.09, first save the input string, the call result and the object's visible fields. Do not start by treating `href` as the only result, and do not immediately attribute a failed setter to the parser. These two lines of investigation were placed on the same troubleshooting sheet in the old notes, but later reviews still found that they needed to be examined separately.

## Starting point left by the old notes

The earliest draft had only a very brief starting point: follow the issue name or call name to `include/ada/url.h`, inspect the declarations around URL and the parser, then return to the call that exhibited the discrepancy. At the time, all that could be confirmed was that this path belonged to the existing h module, and was suitable for code reading and checking historical behavior; no inference about implementation ownership was made from the path name, and no directly copyable command was left.

The working hypotheses in the draft were: if the discrepancy appeared only in the opaque path, the handling rules for a regular pathname might have been applied to a different kind of path; if only some fields were seen to change after the host setter failed, the setter might have changed one field first, then returned failure. Both statements were only hypotheses at the time. For the second statement in particular, the four characters meaning "return failure" do not imply that a partial commit has already occurred.

```text
Rough breakdown at the time
├─ Changes to spaces or output text
│  └─ Check the before-and-after values of opaque path, pathname, href
└─ host setter failure
   └─ Check the fields of the URL object before and after failure is returned
```

This earlier assessment is retained here, because it explains why the initial investigation did not simply combine the two issues. If the review findings do not match these two hypotheses, use the new notes as the source of truth, with no need to modify the old passage.

## What original artifacts to collect first

### opaque path branch

Keep at least three items, and keep them paired with the same input:

1. The raw string passed to the URL processing entry point;
2. The success or failure status returned by the call;
3. The visible text of pathname and href in the result object.

For both successful and failed calls, do not capture only the final href. The observation left by AURL-213 is "Opaque path space result difference in the current version"; the card also separately requires retaining the visible result of one successful call and one failed call. It does not provide a complete output that can replace the on-site original, so the position where spaces appear is not hard-coded here.

```text
Record shape for the same input
raw input
   ├─ call result
   ├─ pathname
   └─ href
```

First compare raw input with pathname, then compare pathname with href. If pathname has already changed, continue by checking the records from the parsing stage; if pathname remains unchanged while href differs, keep the difference confined to the serialization layer. If neither field differs, do not expand the scope further merely because it "looks like a space issue."

### host setter branch

The host setter artifacts must be laid out in chronological order: the visible state of URL before the call, the passed-in host value, the returned status, and the same set of states after the call. At minimum, put scheme, host, port, and pathname in the same record; if any field has no value, record it as empty rather than saving only nonempty fields.

```text
State before call
   ↓
Execute host setter
   ↓
Call succeeded? ── Yes → Save new complete visible state
       │
       No
       ↓
Save complete visible state after failure
       ↓
Compare field by field with state before call
```

Here, "complete" refers only to the fields actually visible in this record; it does not mean that how the internal temporary state was committed has already been proven. After a failure, if all fields are the same as before the call, the result can be recorded as "visible state unchanged"; if only host or port changed, first record the specific field, and do not summarize it as a complete rollback; if there is no snapshot from before the call, leave the assessment blank.

## Decision order

### 1. First confirm whether it is the same input

The successful and failed Opaque path samples must correspond to each other. Check whether the raw strings are the same, whether the call entry points are the same, and whether the results come from the same run. When only one output remains, retain its local significance; do not use it to derive a causal relationship between the two outcomes.

For the host setter, confirm that the setter receives the same host value. Different host inputs cannot be used to compare rollback; changes to scheme must also be recorded separately, because the visible values of scheme, authority, and port may change together. The current material does not provide specific host samples, so do not add an example domain name or port to the record.

### 2. Next, identify which layer the change occurs in

For opaque path, examine the values in the order given by `raw input → pathname → href`. If a change has already occurred between raw input and pathname, the issue is closer to parsing or the path representation; if pathname remains unchanged but href changes, the issue is closer to serialization; if neither changes but the call status differs, first check whether the saved results came from different entry points. Only the order of observation is described here, not an implementation call graph.

For the host setter, follow "fields before the call → failure status → fields after the call". Do not treat a field's absence from the log as evidence that the field did not change. If a column is missing, stop that branch at "cannot compare this field" and continue looking for an object snapshot from the same call.

### 3. Success and failure must be paired

If an opaque path difference has only a successful sample and no failed sample, it can only be recorded as an output sample; if there is only a failed sample, you cannot claim that anything was preserved or lost. Once both samples are available, clearly document where the differences occur in pathname and href.

For host setter rollback, if there is only a failure return value and no pre-call snapshot, this only shows that the setter reported failure. If snapshots from both before and after the call are available, compare them field by field. One matching field does not mean that the entire URL state is the same; one differing field does not mean that all fields were committed.

## When symptoms are mixed

The two branches may occur in sequence within the same test, for example by first processing an opaque path and then calling the host setter. In this case, do not directly use the final href as shared evidence for both operations. First save the state after the first operation, then save the state before the setter call; if there is no snapshot in between, you can only say afterward that "the final results differ", and cannot determine which step caused the change.

```text
Original URL
  │
  ├─ opaque path observations
  │    └─ Save pathname / href
  │
  ├─ Snapshot before host setter
  │    └─ Save scheme / host / port / pathname
  │
  └─ Snapshot after setter returns
       └─ Compare field by field with the snapshot before setter
```

If the first step has already produced a difference, do not work backward from the modified href during the second step to infer the first step's result. If the second step fails, first complete the field comparison for the rollback branch, then go back and mark the first step's output. The sequence itself is part of the captured context.

## Recovery attempts that have failed

Earlier investigations tended to construct a new URL, then compare the new object's output with the old object's output. This approach can help confirm string-level differences, but it cannot prove whether the original object recovered after the host setter failed. The new object has no pre-call state and did not experience the same setter failure, so it can only serve as supporting evidence, not as a replacement for before-and-after snapshots.

Another action that can easily cause confusion is copying only the final href, then reparsing it to validate the opaque path. The reparsed object has already undergone a second transformation; if the difference arose between pathname and href, the second parse will erase the distinctions between the original stages. Keep the original input and the first output, and treat reparsing only as a separate sample.

If the existing logs contain only the final text, recovery efforts should go no further than filling in the input, return status, and object fields from that same call. Do not use successful results for a regular path to fill in a failed sample for an opaque path, and do not use an object after a successful setter call as the state after a failed setter call.

## On-call branch table

| Observed behavior | Check first | Stop condition |
|---|---|---|
| Space differences in opaque path output | The pairing among raw input, pathname, and href | Do not judge whether spaces were preserved or lost with only one sample |
| pathname already differs, and href also differs | Changes from the input to pathname | Do not identify the stage where the difference occurred without the original input |
| pathname is the same, but href differs | The visible text before and after serialization | Do not combine samples without results from the same object |
| host setter returns failure | scheme, host, port, and pathname before and after the call | Do not claim rollback without a pre-call snapshot |
| Only one field differs after failure | Record the specific field and return status | Do not generalize to the overall state without the other fields |
| Both types of behavior occur in the same call chain | Snapshots between each operation | Do not attribute the issue to a particular step without intermediate snapshots |

The stop conditions in the table are not a new conclusion, they simply prevent missing original evidence from being treated as "no change". The record can stop at a single comparable field, with the remaining fields separately marked as not obtained.

## Entry points and version differences

When starting from `include/ada/url.h`, first confirm that the declaration you are looking at still corresponds to the source code state used for this investigation. The path can tell a reviewer where to start looking in the areas adjacent to URL, parser, opaque path, pathname, and setter, but it cannot replace runtime results. Do not mix another build artifact or an old object snapshot into the current sample just because the path names are the same.

The safety routing for AURL-213 occurred at 2025-10-09, and then entered In Progress; it corresponds to the result difference in the opaque path. It is cited here only for navigation and to anchor the observation target; the card status is not treated as a test conclusion.

AURL-230 left a documentation review record in 2025-10-31; the public comment explicitly stated that one point in the Full host-setter transaction rollback remained unconfirmed; it entered In Progress again on 11 month 3 day. This gap is still being retained: there is currently no evidence showing which dependency, which job, or which pinned version changed the result, nor is there evidence that all fields after the failure returned to their pre-call values. When comparing the artifacts available in the previous round, update only the jobs or pinned versions that actually changed; do not treat the entire dependency list as content for this page.

## Current wording after review

During review, first add the visible success/failure results for the opaque path to the same set of records, then record the host setter's before-and-after-call states in a separate set. Both sets start from the same local entry point, but each retains its own object and return state. The only determinations currently available are:

- The opaque path requires comparing the pathname and href from successful and failed calls;
- the host setter requires using the complete visible fields before and after the call to determine whether the state changed;
- the path declaration is navigation material and cannot by itself replace these two types of observed results;
- the rollback boundary indicated by AURL-230 still has one unconfirmed point.

If a new review fills in only one of the sets, the other remains unconfirmed. Do not, just to make this page appear closed out, rewrite "no pre-call snapshot was obtained," "only the final href," or "the success and failure inputs are not paired" as successful verification.

## Record format

For each new result, just continue using the local format below; do not fill missing fields with guesses:

```text
Object: opaque path / host setter
Input: <original input or host setter parameters>
Result: <success or failure return>
Before call: <visible fields; required for host setter, fill in for opaque path according to what was obtained>
After call: <pathname, href, or the fields in the same group as the host setter>
Comparison: <specific fields that changed; for fields that cannot be compared, specify which original is missing>
```

For opaque path, `Before call` may have no URL object field, but the original input and output must be kept separate; for host setter, if there are no before-call fields, no rollback determination can be made. If both types of objects appear, fill in two sections separately, and do not copy the final href into the setter's field comparison.

## Marginal notes still remaining at the bottom of the page

- This path is currently sufficient only for local declarations and adjacent navigation.
- Experience with ordinary pathname cannot automatically be applied to opaque path.
- The result of reconstructing URL cannot replace the original object's post-failure state.
- The success/failure samples for AURL-213 must remain paired; the unconfirmed items for AURL-230 should not be deleted for now.

When new facts become available next time, prioritize filling in the missing items in the original input, return status, or before-call snapshot. If only the final text is obtained, leave it in the corresponding branch; do not elevate it to a conclusion about the entire URL object.

# Aggregator Offset Proposal

The aggregator's offset is initially treated as a single continuous position. The question here is whether, after components have written to the same URL object, the position in the aggregated result can still point to the original segment; do not broaden this yet to serialization format or caller compatibility issues.

The initial proposal is to retain a unified cumulative position after the aggregator finishes concatenating the components, and have all subsequent writes continue calculating from this position. This keeps changes to pathname, search, and hash on the same calculation path, without storing a separate set of boundaries for each component. This assessment depends on one premise: replacing a component will not make previously recorded positions meaningless.

There are two options. The first is to calculate the offset once at the aggregator's output boundary, which keeps the changes localized but cannot determine whether records after an intermediate replacement remain usable. The second is to recalculate after every component write; the boundaries are more straightforward, at the cost of requiring the aggregator to know more component state. The preference here is the former; as long as the length before output is correct, the internal records should remain reusable.

When trying it out, first inspect the declarations near `include/ada/url_aggregator.h`, and check the cumulative position while tracing the writes to `set_pathname`, `search`, and `hash` in sequence. If an empty component or successive replacements makes the position uninterpretable, withdraw the unified cumulative-position approach and instead read the value again at output.

Still undecided: whether `after` and `length` are sufficient to express all component boundaries; whether `validate` should participate in the check before writing or after aggregation.
versions.change_summary: Record the initial preference for a unified cumulative position

# Aggregator Offset Proposal

The previous proposal treated offset as a value derived at the end of aggregation, assuming that as long as the final length was correct, replacing components would not affect previously recorded positions. That claim remains here because it explains why the original plan was to change just one cumulative position; there is not yet enough evidence from actual objects to support it.

Later, at the investigation entry point for AURL-217, the issue showed up as Aggregator offset output that could not be reproduced consistently. The card did not provide the full call chain, but it made the assumption that "the final length just needs to be correct" less safe: inconsistent output at least indicates that position recording and the order of component writes need to be examined separately. The card later went through rollback_checked; that only shows that the rollback state was checked and cannot be taken as an implementation conclusion.

There are still three earlier approaches to compare.

- **Output-side accumulation.** Keep the v1 approach and use the total `length` to provide a single position once aggregation is complete. This keeps the changes small and makes it easy to treat `after` as a single boundary. The drawback is that when search or hash is added after pathname is rewritten, there is no separate position to consult to establish what earlier records mean.
- **Per-component recording.** Save relative positions as pathname, search, and hash are each written, and only convert them to final positions during aggregation. This separates replacement from concatenation, but makes the records themselves part of the aggregator's state.
- **Recalculate after writing.** Do not store intermediate offsets; recalculate them from the current components after every change. This avoids old records, but pushes the decision to a later point; if `validate` needs to see the pre-write state, that order may not be appropriate.

For this round, the provisional choice is still output-side accumulation—not because it has been proven correct, but because the aggregation object's local interface can be checked near the header first, making it easy to keep the trial scope limited. The planned check order is now: replace pathname first, then append search and hash separately, and finally compare the positions corresponding to `after` and `length`. Do not treat matching output from a single run as evidence that the component records are equivalent.

The conditions for dropping this approach are also more specific: if existing offsets cannot be reinterpreted before and after the same component is replaced; if the point at which `validate` participates changes what the positions mean; or if the behavior in AURL-217 still cannot be reproduced consistently with this sequence, stop pursuing output-side accumulation. At that point, try per-component recording first, rather than continuing to add special-case branches to the single variable.

Open questions: whether empty components retain their own boundaries; whether the aggregator should expose intermediate records; and whether writes to components other than pathname share the same `after` semantics.

# Aggregator Offset Proposal

This proposal retains the original direction of treating offset as "a single cumulative position after aggregation completes". At the time, it seemed lightweight enough: the aggregator did not need to maintain separate state for pathname, search, and hash, and the writing side only needed each subsequent fragment to continue from the end of the previous one. The initial expectation was that component values could change, but the aggregated object would always have a single, interpretable progression of positions.

That expectation later ran up against the behavior in AURL-217. That entry records that Aggregator offset output cannot be reproduced consistently, not an implementation defect with an established cause. The card's routine-check description calls for following the maintainer's steps to inspect "Aggregator offset integrity" and leaving sections blank where evidence is missing. It does not provide a complete chain sufficient to determine a fix, so this draft cannot directly attribute the inconsistent reproduction to any one component, nor present the status from a single check as a verified fix.

The original draft's mistake was not proposing cumulative positions, but treating "the final length is the same" as a substitute for proof that the positions still meant the same thing. If pathname is replaced and search or hash is then added, the output `length` may look reasonable; whether a previously recorded offset still corresponds to the same span of content is another matter. These two questions were not separated at the time, which led to a preference for performing the additional calculation only at the output stage.

## Approaches Planned for Trial at the Time

The output-stage accumulation approach uses `after` as the sole value for advancing the position: after each component write completes, the current cumulative value becomes the starting point for the next write; once aggregation is complete, the result is obtained using the total `length`. Its appeal is straightforward: no additional records, and no requirement for the aggregator to expose internal component state. The v1 conclusion was that this approach was sufficient as long as the final result was contiguous.

That conclusion is still retained as originally stated, both because it was the central judgment in this proposal at the time and because the scope of changes then did indeed center on that judgment. It does not mean component replacement can now be declared safe on that basis. In particular, when components occur in a different order, a component is empty, or a component is rewritten, continuity in the total length does not automatically tell us what happens to the old offset.

The second approach is component-level recording: pathname, search, and hash each record their relative positions when written, and the aggregation stage converts those positions to positions in the final object. It separates "which component changed" from "where the final position is", at the cost of having records travel with the object and making the aggregator's state more complex than with output-stage accumulation. The original draft did not choose it, mainly because there was no desire at the time to expand a local offset problem into recordkeeping for all components.

The third approach is post-write recalculation. It does not trust historical records, instead deriving positions again from the current result after every component change. This approach seems reliable, but if `validate` needs to distinguish old values from new values during a write, the timing of recalculation itself affects the judgment. It cannot establish correctness simply by "calculating once more at the end"; for that reason, it was not adopted as the default approach either.

There is also a smaller-scale approach: add compensation only for changes to pathname, assuming that search and hash will not change earlier positions. This approach was raised during discussion but was not included in the trial. It treats component names as behavioral boundaries, neither accounting for subsequent concatenation nor avoiding burying offset rules in a special case. Even if output-stage accumulation is ultimately retained, it should not be kept working through a pathname-specific patch.

## Narrowing the Scope After the Check

AURL-217 was later marked rollback_checked. This action halted the original plan to "move straight into a trial": first confirm that the object after rollback is still observed through the same entry point, and only then discuss expanding the changes. It did not answer which stage should produce the offset, nor did it state that the problem occurs only in the setter, at aggregation output, or during serialization.

Another point that needs correction is the role of the path. `include/ada/url_aggregator.h` can serve as a reference for local declarations and for navigating nearby code to locate interfaces around the names of the aggregator, `set_pathname`, `search`, `hash`, `after`, `length`, and `validate`; it cannot by itself establish where the implementation belongs, nor prove that all writes go through the same position calculation. The original draft treated the header as a sufficient anchor, which was overly optimistic. It is now retained as an entry point for inspection, but is no longer used to infer the full call relationships.

The trial scope should therefore be narrowed to a set of distinguishable component orderings, rather than claiming to cover all URL changes. First examine the case where a pathname write is followed by search; then a pathname write followed by hash; only then check whether `after` and `length` can still describe the same boundary when search and hash appear consecutively. For each case, record only whether the offset provided by the aggregated object is reproducible, without filling in caller behavior that has not been observed.

## The Original Proposal's Choice and Trade-offs

This draft still chooses to retain output-stage accumulation as a candidate for now, rather than immediately switching to component-level recording. The reason is that it allows the trial to remain limited to local checks of aggregation results, avoiding adding storage fields to every component before the call relationships are known. This choice is a judgment about cost, not a conclusion about correctness.

The costs should also be stated clearly. Output-stage accumulation collapses intermediate history into final positions, so investigation can only work backward from the current result; once a replacement leaves an old boundary without an associated object, the aggregator has no independent record to explain it. Component-level recording is the opposite: it makes boundaries easier to locate, but may tie every write to additional state. Post-write recalculation leaves the complexity in timing and validation order. The available material does not directly establish any of the three as the winner.

The original plan was to use "the total length is unchanged, so the offset should also be unchanged" as the pass condition for output-stage accumulation, but that condition is now retained only as an earlier proposal. The same total length can come from different component combinations and cannot establish that the offset still points to the same content. Anyone reusing this proposal must not treat that statement as an acceptance criterion.

## Stop Conditions

The output-stage accumulation approach should stop if any of the following occurs, rather than continuing to add compensation:

- After pathname is rewritten, existing positions cannot be explained in terms of the current aggregation result;
- Adding search or hash produces unstable offsets for the same observation sequence;
- Changing the ordering of `validate` changes the boundary represented by `after`;
- Checks after rollback still yield only intermittent results, making it impossible to distinguish whether differences are caused by component order or the recording method.

After stopping, first compare component-level recording with post-write recalculation, rather than returning to pathname-specific compensation. If both require caller information, the proposal should remain local to the aggregator and should not expand the behavior in AURL-217 into a public interface change.

## Open Questions

Whether empty components should have visible boundaries remains undecided. Whether `after` is the end of a component, the start of the next component, or merely an internal cumulative value is also left unresolved here. Which layer of object `length` should represent before and after replacement likewise cannot be determined by local names in the header.

This document has not been rewritten as a new proposal in light of subsequent checks. Its practical value is in explaining why the old approach chose output-stage accumulation, where it conflated length with position, and what kind of special-case patch should not be used when backing it out.
versions.change_summary: Correct the old assumption that length is equivalent to position; retain the old approach

# Performance Lab Entry Point Migration

This index has long sat alongside the Performance Lab's capacity records. It was not originally a complete migration plan; it merely put in one place the old entry points that would still be opened, the alternative locations under trial, and the callers that could be confirmed to remain in use. Early readers often treated names newly added to the directory as evidence that migration was complete; this is also why the old paragraphs were not deleted later.

The Performance Lab itself focuses on capacity baselines, resource curves, and degradation localization, with its own schedule, maintainers, and exit criteria. This page does not explain every curve on its behalf, nor does it collect all similar pages. A bypass with the same name is still treated as a bypass unless the original index already states its relationship. See DOC-32 for the maintainer mapping elsewhere; this page retains only the records that need to be consulted during entry migration.

The earliest recorded judgment was: continue along `setter rollback`, or split `capture group` out separately. At the time, the failure exits of the two branches looked different, so the latter was favored. This judgment remains below and should not be read as a completed structural change; at the time, not all consumers were listed, and the current callers for `punycode` had not all been found.

> Old note: Whether migration is complete is confirmed by actual consumers, not by whether a new entry appears in the directory.
>
> Old note: When rolling back, restore the old entry first; discuss the split-out portion later.

The first note still applies. The second is retained only in its original context. Later, when someone acted on the second note, the problem was not whether it was possible to return to the old name, but that there was no original request after returning, so it was impossible to determine whether the failure was still present. Making "restore the old entry" the sole completion criterion would hide this gap.

```text
old entry ── retained ──> known consumer
   │                    │
   │                    ├── trial alternative location
   │                    └── on inconsistency, return to old entry
   │
   └── store original input alongside first failure

alternative location: URLPattern
another processing track: canonicalization
```

The two lines in the diagram are simply two names from the index; this does not mean they are interchangeable. `URLPattern` is the alternative location written during the trial; `canonicalization` is the processing track listed separately. Early versions placed the two very close together, making them read like the same migration batch; this is one of the easiest misreadings caused by the old index. Later records provided no basis for merging them, so they are still recorded separately.

## Fill in the old entry first, rather than changing the name first

When handling a migration batch, first fill in three things on the old-entry side of the index: which consumer is still using it, where the original input can be obtained, and what the first failure was. Here, "consumer" refers only to the one already confirmed in this page or related materials; do not infer a series of similar calls from the name.

If all you have is a cleaned-up screenshot, leave the old entry marked unverified. A screenshot can show that someone saw an anomaly at the time, but it cannot substitute for the original request or determine whether the rollback restored the original behavior. A later record stopped exactly here: the attachment contained only a screenshot, and the original request corresponding to the exit entry was not attached. Do not change this type of entry to "no longer an issue," and do not delete the old entry just because the alternative location can be opened.

When the original failure is missing, the index may say "awaiting sample," but do not fill the gap with a guess. In one case, the first-round material after a fix was required to be retained alongside the original failure; it can show only what the first post-fix record looked like, not infer the route of every prior call. When there is no original request between the old failure and the first post-fix round, they remain two separate pieces of material.

The old entry also has a coarse classification: readable, available for trial, rollbackable, and unverified. It is neither a state machine nor a release commitment. It only helps the person taking over avoid interpreting "can see the page" as "can reproduce." Readable means the index can still locate the entry; available for trial means there is a known consumer Fang Ke who can switch to the alternative location; rollbackable means the old entry has not been deleted; and unverified means the key material consists only of screenshots or fragments, or lacks caller confirmation. Early pages mixed these cases together under "in migration," which is no longer sufficient.

## Trial only one consumer at a time

The alternative location does not cover all callers at once. First select one consumer already identified in the index, move it from the old entry to `URLPattern`, and keep the old entry readable. For the comparison, retain the same input, the same consumer, and the first visible result; the only change should come from this entry replacement. The purpose is not to produce a general conclusion, but to prevent other changes in the resource curve from being treated as consequences of the migration.

If a different result appears after the trial, reconnect the old entry first. Reconnecting it does not mean deleting the trial record: the original input, the result from the alternative location, and the result after restoring the old entry all remain alongside the same batch. Without all three items, the index should say only "trial not closed out." Do not use a later cleaned-up green screenshot to overwrite the initial failure, and do not treat the state of the second call as a substitute for the first failure.

There was often an inaccurate shortcut at this step: attributing the inconsistency in `canonicalization` directly to the alternative location. The existing material supports only checking them separately; it does not support that attribution. If the inconsistency occurs on this processing track, first stop expanding the trial for that consumer; if it remains inconsistent after restoring the old entry, retain it as an old-entry-side issue. Neither outcome means that the other callers can be migrated as well.

The split of `capture group` should be viewed in the same way. It was originally intended to record the failure exits separately, not to serve as an alternative entry confirmed by all callers. A consumer Fang Ke continuing the trial after the split does not mean that another old call can skip the original entry and connect directly. When the index lacks enough material, it is better to write only "caller has not replied."

## The old rollback wording and the limitations added later

The old wording was "When `canonicalization` is inconsistent, restore the old entry and look again using the original input." This sentence is still useful because it says not to keep expanding the migration when results are inconsistent. But it omitted one prerequisite: the original input must exist. When there is only a screenshot or an organized result, the restoration action can be performed, but the recheck cannot be completed; in that situation, the entry cannot be marked as verified.

Another old wording was "Only stop maintaining the old path when the alternative entry, caller confirmation, and historical lookup are all valid." It is still worth consulting during directory cleanup, but "historical lookup is valid" does not specify what was looked up. Do not now interpret it as merely finding an old link. At minimum, it must be possible to identify the consumer that the link points to, the entry it uses, and whether the original input or failure material has been retained. If any one of these is missing, the old path remains in the index.

Some entries also say, "Each maintainer answers only for the segment they own." This wording is retained because the Performance Lab does have its own maintenance boundary; however, it must not be used to push missing caller confirmation elsewhere. The person responsible for the entry can explain its status, and the person responsible for the consumer can confirm the actual migration. When the two sides have no overlapping material, leave the item unverified rather than assembling a completion conclusion.

When confirmation about a maintenance entry arrives, update only the corresponding field and leave the other entries in their original states. This practice was later reflected in AURLA-002: confirmation is not a re-acceptance of the entire index. This card had previously been impossible to check because the person on duty was unavailable, and later stalled again because there was only a screenshot and no original failure; both pauses show that updating a field and solving the problem are not the same thing.

## Several batch notes that were not cleared

- **The old entry remains, and the alternative location has been entered.** These entries can begin a limited trial, but they cannot be marked complete just because the directory contains two names at the same time. Most of the original migration notes belong to this category.
- **The alternative location has a first-round record, but the old failure has no original request.** The first post-fix record should remain alongside the original failure. AURLA-005 once stopped at the point where the consumer still lacked a failure sample; this limitation still applies, and later first-round material must not be used to fill it into a complete reproduction.
- **The second person can reproduce only with the material in the card.** AURLA-019 used this approach: the gap was left directly beside the original step. This is useful for exposing what the original index omitted, but not for generalizing the second person's result to all consumers.
- **The original owner was replaced.** One migration-related record was handed to a teammate in the same group because the original owner was on leave. After the handoff, first confirm where the old entry, the alternative location, and the existing attachments are; do not write the handoff itself as migration success.

These batches did not form a continuous cleanup effort. There were pauses between them, as well as updates that filled in only one field. The index preserves this untidiness so that later readers can see that some migrations were rolled back because results were inconsistent, some could not be assessed at all because the original failure was not saved, and some were simply waiting for the caller to reply. Compressing them into one overall "migrated/not migrated" status would instead lose the information most needed when restoring the old path.

## Continuing with this index now

First find a consumer that is still clearly identified on the old-entry side. If an entry lists only the alternative name and no consumer, add the consumer first and do not switch. When the original input is already in the material, retain it and record the first visible result; when there is no original input and only a screenshot, retain the screenshot's source and limit the trial to "unverified."

Then move only that consumer to `URLPattern`. Do not also modify `canonicalization`, and do not group the two as one item merely because both names appear. If the results differ, restore the old entry; if the original input still cannot be obtained after restoration, record the restoration action only and do not call it a completed reproduction. If the results are consistent, that shows only that this consumer's trial has not yet produced a difference; it does not provide a basis for migrating the remaining callers.

Before actually stopping maintenance of an old path, the index should still retain the correspondence among the alternative location, the confirmed consumers, and the historical material. Here, "stop maintaining" means only that the old entry is no longer listed as a work item for continued migration; it does not mean that the old link, old screenshot, or old paragraph disappears from the knowledge base. Keep the old material, especially explanations later shown to be impossible to check back; they remind the person taking over not to substitute the directory's appearance for caller confirmation.

The current callers for `punycode` have still not all been collected on this page. It has therefore not been classified under `URLPattern`, nor has it been treated as an example of `canonicalization`. If a clearly identified consumer and the original input are obtained later, add a separate entry beside the corresponding old entry; do not rewrite the early two-branch judgment to make the old version look as if it already knew the answer at the time.

This index still retains one adjacent question at the end: when the resource curve changes, is the cause the entry replacement, the consumer load, or some other recording condition? The existing material is insufficient to separate these causes. The migration batch is responsible only for retaining the original comparison before and after the entry replacement; capacity baselines and degradation localization continue to be handled by the Performance Lab's own records.
versions.change_summary: Filled in records for trials, rollbacks, and missing samples

# Performance Lab Maintainer Map

Performance Lab work items once routed exit actions and temporary coverage through the same on-call intake. That intake is suitable for receiving issues and filling in handoff information, but it should not draw conclusions on behalf of the long-term technical owner. The table below lists the actual handoff items separately; where no person is registered, leave the slot blank rather than temporarily assigning it to whoever is on call.

| Item | Long-term owner | Intake or escalation point | What to leave with the handoff |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Run records, resource curves, and degradation investigation | Not yet registered | Project maintenance intake | Records from this run, along with the curves or diagnostic points being compared |
| Exit actions | Not yet registered | Project maintenance intake | Current exit conditions, unfinished actions, and points that need further confirmation |
| Temporary coverage actions | Person providing temporary coverage (on-duty shift only) | Project maintenance intake | Coverage scope, parts already handled, and the unfilled long-term owner slot for handing the work back |
| Page body and attachments | Project maintenance intake | Project maintenance intake | Page changes and materials still attached to the project |

Temporary coverage is not another name for the long-term owner. The person on duty can bring existing records into a handoff-ready state and route exit actions to the maintenance intake. For judgments about resource curves, causes of degradation, or long-term trade-offs, leave the owner field blank if no owner is registered in the table. Do not cite the intake as the source of a technical conclusion just because it has received the message.

Exit actions are listed separately so they are not obscured by a stint of temporary coverage. If someone only takes over actions during their shift, the handoff should state where that coverage ends. If the exit conditions still have no corresponding owner, the maintenance intake is only responsible for preserving that gap in the record. When a long-term owner is confirmed later, add them to that cell; do not backfill it as a judgment already made during an on-call shift.

# Performance Lab Dual-Record Postmortem

At one point, the Performance Lab's current entry point held records from two revisions at the same time. It did not indicate that they came from different revisions, so people reviewing them through that entry point would treat either one as the current revision. No material was lost. The problem was that old records still appeared in the same location, and the entry point itself did not provide enough information to establish which record came first.

The first comparison during the incident recorded only one difference: the capture group did not match the old record. At the time, the difference was initially attributed to scheme transition, on the assumption that the content shown at the entry point had already been through the same round of conversion. That judgment was retained in the record; subsequent checks did not confirm it as the cause.

The incident timeline lacks complete timestamps and can only be ordered by the actions recorded:

- First, two records were seen side by side at the current entry point; the capture group in one differed from the old record.
- Next, the conversion behavior was reviewed against the old record, and the record noted that punycode could be restored.
- The same conclusion was not reached for the changes to dot segment, and the cause remained undocumented.
- Finally, the incident record was retained at its version from that point, and further retries were stopped.

The scope of impact could not be determined at the time. The entry point would give consumers inconsistent records, but the incident notes did not confirm which consumers had actually retrieved the old revision and which had only seen the entry point without going on to use it. This is not enough to attribute changes in adjacent services to this incident.

Stopping retries did not confirm that the two sets of material had been merged; it was intended to avoid continuing to overwrite the incident state without new observations. The retained version still carries the initial scheme transition judgment. It is therefore suitable for explaining why no further action was taken at the time, but not as the sole description of the current entry point. The observed recovery of punycode only shows that that part can return to its old behavior; it does not explain the difference in dot segment.

Two timestamps are still missing: when the two revisions began sharing the current entry point, and when consumers were first affected. Without the original usage records, the latter can only remain marked as unknown.

# Release Automation FAQ

This page collects three types of questions users have repeatedly raised during releases: where to start, what is meant by the current revision, and where to hand off the context. They concern `.github/workflows`, the release queue, artifact versions, and withdrawal windows; don't conflate these different things based on a single success or failure.

Start with `docs/adj-fuzz/faq/fuzz-release-automation-three-consumer-questions.md`. This entry point holds the FAQ and attachments and is still maintained by fuzz · Release Automation. Users who only need to retrieve the original materials don't need to explain the main project's behavior first.

**What does "current revision" mean?**

The revision here is the version of the page or materials the question is based on, not any passing result from a later rerun. When submitting the context, record the revision at the time, the first visible result, and the release queue it was in. If you also mention an artifact version, list it separately: the queue having advanced does not mean a particular artifact is the version currently available to fetch, much less that the withdrawal window is still open.
