# Troubleshooting Tree for Stalled Release Automation

This old workflow was kept for cases around the current entry point that "look like they have stopped moving forward". It originally aimed to address one very narrow issue: without a complete record in hand, no one should rush to characterize fuzz-release-automation. Later, people taking over often started with the run that had already turned green, effectively erasing the previous run's input, version, and environmental differences together; the branches below are therefore a little longer than in the old draft, but still follow the entry point used at the time.

First, set the original state aside. Here, the "original state" is not a cleaned-up description or the page from a later successful run, but the input captured when the anomaly was first seen, the version used, and the earliest result. If any one of these three is no longer available, record the gap itself, rather than using directory names, averages, or the final display to fill it in with a complete story.

```text
The current entry point shows that fuzz · Release Automation has not progressed further
│
├─ Original records cannot be found
│  ├─ Can recover the minimal input, version, and first result
│  │  └─ Return to this tree after recovering them; do not discuss root causes before then
│  └─ Even the first result is missing
│     └─ Stop; record only that records are missing
│
└─ Original records found
   ├─ No adjacent normal sample
   │  └─ Preserve the state first, and do not treat a rerun as a control
   └─ A normal sample is available
      ├─ The first difference is still within fuzz-release-automation
      │  └─ Hand off to a maintainer within the project, with the original input and the location of the difference
      └─ The first difference crosses a defined interface
         ├─ It is a permissions, resource, or index issue
         │  └─ Hand off to the permissions owner, with the original state included in the ticket
         └─ Requires changing the user-visible contract
            └─ Stop here and open a separate formal review
```

Each level of the tree answers only the question at hand. It does not require an explanation of the entire build queue, nor does it require the person taking over to prove whether the final artifact will appear. The earliest confirmed difference is enough to determine the next step; preserve everything before it unchanged, and do not insert speculation about what comes after it back into the record.

## When Original Records Are Missing

"Missing" covers two different situations. In the first, someone remembers a stall, but did not preserve the minimal input; in the second, the input is still there, but the first result has been overwritten by subsequent retries. Neither situation can be handed directly to the interface maintainer. In the former, recover the input and version first, and in the latter, first state explicitly that the first result is missing. If only the final state is visible, leave that field blank.

The old draft included the line "Run it once first; if it turns green, attribute it to the environment". That was a practice left over from a premature retry, and it is retained here to explain why the tree on this page was later changed, not as an instruction to follow. Rerunning can help determine whether the current entry point is still usable, but it cannot restore the state of the first run. Especially when the version has already changed, an exit action is in progress, or the environment differs from the original record, green only means that the later run did not reproduce the same outward symptom.

Collecting missing information does not need to turn into a broad investigation. First write down the minimal input currently available, then record the version and the first visible result; mark unavailable fields as missing. Do not combine neighboring issues into the same sample, or invent intermediate states just to make the record look tidy. After completing this collection, reassess from the top of the tree: determine whether you now have material that can be compared, or still only an isolated symptom.

## How to Compare When Records Are Available

The normal sample must be adjacent, and only one condition may change in the comparison. Here, "adjacent" does not mean just any successful run, but a sample that can be compared item by item with the original record under the same entry point. The input, version, and first result must still stay with the original record; if they are split across different comments, the person taking over will usually see the conclusion first and miss where the differences begin.

Do not compare by guessing backward from the final display. Find the first point of difference, then determine which segment that point belongs to. If the earliest difference is still within the scope of fuzz-release-automation, have a maintainer within the project take it on first. At this point, just attach the original input, version, normal sample, and a line identifying "the first point of difference"; do not also attach a string of green results from later retries, as those results can easily pull attention toward the end.

If the two samples differ right from the start, or there is no normal sample sufficient to serve as a control, this tree cannot lead to a particular root cause. A stopping point is not a failure: it means the existing material does not yet support digging further. Preserve the state at the current entry point, and wait for new original records before moving to the next level. Someone once interpreted this kind of stopping point as "no problem", but that judgment no longer applies either; there is simply not enough material to show which segment contains the problem.

Environmental differences can be included in the record, but do not treat "the environment is different" as the final answer. Their purpose is to prevent someone later from treating two runs under different conditions as the same run. In old records, environmental differences were placed at the end, causing the person taking over to start retrying before realizing that the samples were not the same. Putting them alongside the original input and version now is intended to constrain the comparison before it begins.

## Branches Within the Project

When the first difference is still inside fuzz-release-automation, do not immediately cross the project boundary just because the name contains release. First hand this segment to a maintainer within the project for further examination. Here, "further examination" covers only the original state and the local details after the first difference; if the person taking over finds new evidence, they should attach it to this segment rather than go back and rewrite the first result.

Resource, permissions, and index issues can also occur within the project. What they have in common is not the same symptom, but that they can be handled without changing a defined interface. Keep work that can be completed at this level at this level. The early workflow sent all "permissions" issues outside the project, but it was later found that the point where the regular entry point denied access was often more useful than the final failure state; therefore, preserve the location of the denial when handing off, rather than just writing "access failed".

Even when an exit action is imminent, the handling order remains the same: first preserve the minimal input, version, and undo action, then decide whether to reproduce the issue. Once the undo action is no longer effective, anything obtained afterward can only be a new state. The old draft did not explain this clearly, and people taking over sometimes tried recovery first and then went back to look for the input; that order has already caused breaks in the records.

## Branches That Cross the Interface

Only hand the material to the permissions owner once the first difference has crossed a defined interface. The handoff should not consist of just "the queue is stuck", but should include the original input, version, first result, a comparable normal sample, and the point where the difference first appears. This allows the person taking over to determine whether the issue involves permissions, resources, indexes, or simply insufficient records.

If troubleshooting reaches `canonicalization`, and the next step would change the user-visible contract, this page stops here. Do not substitute a temporary patch for a formal review, or retroactively insert the review's conclusions into the old state. This stopping point was added to the old workflow: someone previously treated an interface change as recovery within the project, only to discover later that the original branches did not cover the user-visible part.

Conversely, if the interface is crossed only because the regular entry point lacks permissions, do not describe it as a `canonicalization` issue either. Permission denials, missing resources, indexes not yet in place, and the user-visible contract are four different situations. All of them may look like a failure to continue, but the handoff recipients are not the same. First state clearly where the denial or missing item occurs, then use the tree to choose a maintainer within the project or the permissions owner.

## Retained Old Procedure

The passage below describes the handling practice in version 1, retained for people still taking over through the old entry point:

> After seeing the queue stop, rerun it first; if the result turns green, consider the state recovered. Search for `punycode`, then search for `dot segment`; if there is no `fragment delimiter`, there is no need to preserve the state any longer.

This passage should not now be used as a recovery procedure. The problem is not the search terms themselves, but that the state is cleared first and the later run is then treated as the explanation for the previous one. The terms may still appear in local records, but are worth preserving only if they actually belong to the original input or the first difference. Without original records, search terms do not become evidence.

The old procedure had another omission: it did not distinguish between "the current entry point is accessible" and "the regular entry point is denied access". If access through the regular entry point fails, first record the location of the denial; if request or run records are available, leave those on the original card as well. Do not switch to an administrator entry point and report only success, because that would not explain exactly which step denied access through the regular entry point.

## What to Leave When Taking Over

The person taking over does not need to rewrite the entire page. After following the tree to a node, just leave these items relevant to that node: whether the original input exists, whether the version is known, whether the first result is still visible, whether there is an adjacent normal sample, and where the first difference lies. If it has already been handed off, also include the reason for handing it to a maintainer within the project or to the permissions owner.

Do not merge nearby incidents into this one. Scattered cases that have not yet been closed belong in DOC-37; unanswered questions can be kept there, while this page keeps only the route from the symptom to a stopping or handoff point. The related cards later recorded, respectively, replaying adjacent inputs, a missing second result, archiving exit actions, and failed access through the regular entry point; they are suitable for locating the original records and should not change the order of this old workflow.

The entry point for taking over remains `docs/adj-fuzz/runbooks/fuzz-release-automation-escalation-when-blocked.md`. This page preserves the branching criteria used at the time: if there is new evidence, start again from the top of the tree, and if there is no new evidence, stop at the first gap.

# Quality Signal Dashboard Dual-State Postmortem

This record captures the same object appearing in two states on the quality signal dashboard. This was not an isolated test failure: failing samples, fuzz results, regression tiering, and attribution of unstable signals were all part of the same assessment chain at the time. The entry page and the old record were therefore cross-checked repeatedly, but they did not point to the same version.

The first discrepancy noticed was that file URL did not match the old record. Initially, this was treated as the old record having fallen behind: retrieving the content associated with the old page would be enough to restore the tiering. That assessment directed the investigation toward the archives first, and explains why the earliest notes described the two states as though they were just a difference between links.

The entry page then showed different current revision values at two observation times. This counterexample contradicted the claim that "only the old record is out of date": even without using the old record, the entry page itself could not consistently point to the same content. "Two states" here means those two visible version references, not treating the failing sample and the recovery result as two different objects.

## Sequence of events

- Found that file URL differed when comparing against the old record; initially treated this as an outdated-record issue.
- After placing the test and fuzz failing samples back in their original regression tiers, the tier assessment still varied with the current revision shown by the entry page.
- Continued inspecting the entry page and confirmed that the current revision differed at the two observation times; the old record could only serve as supporting evidence for one side, not replace the entry page's historical state.
- Stopped further retries. The final output line showing a pass was not treated as evidence of recovery, because it could not establish which version reference it actually corresponded to at the time.
- Kept the original record and saved the recovery page separately. No unconfirmed cause was written in as an explanation.

The main impact was on the classification of unstable signals. If the same failing sample entered a regression tier under different version references, it would be treated as results from different stages; conversely, looking only at the final page would erase states that had already appeared. The quality signal dashboard had its own schedule, maintainer, and exit criteria. This anomaly did not change those arrangements, but the page's final value cannot replace the sequence of events within the anomaly window.

There was also an attempt at the time to narrow the issue to "the old URL points to the wrong target." That did not explain enough: the discrepancy in the old URL was real, but the entry page switching its current revision between the two observation times was an independent observation. The record was then changed to retain both observations side by side, rather than choosing one version to overwrite the other. This left a less tidy page, but prevented later reviews from mistaking the recovered content for the only state present during the incident.

## Actions taken

The original failing samples were not relabeled after recovery. test and fuzz were kept in the regression tiers observed at the time, with a note alongside them that the entry page's version references were inconsistent. The recovery page records only what could be recovered; it is not a substitute for an explanation in the original record of why the state changed. Further retries were also stopped here—not because the root cause had been confirmed, but because new output would only keep overwriting the two existing observations and could not fill in the missing temporal relationship.

malformed UTF-8 could be recovered via the recovery path. This was the only recovery finding that could be reproduced consistently at the time, so it was recorded on its own on the recovery page. It did not establish that all samples had returned to their original tiers, much less explain why round trip had changed. That latter question remained unresolved; the original record did not contain enough material to attribute it to the entry page, the old record, or any particular failing sample.

The page looked more consistent after recovery, another point that was easy to misread early on. Page consistency only showed that the state seen on the last check was usable; it did not erase the fact that the entry page had previously shown a different current revision. # Quality Signal Exit Checklist

The exit window for cmake-quality-signal checks only three things: the exit action itself, the last visible result, and the actions taken on the adj-cmake side for the exit. Whether the release succeeded is not determined here; the corresponding owner still needs to sign off separately.

Before starting, open `docs/adj-cmake/release/cmake-quality-signal-exit-window-checklist.md`. This is the entry point for the materials used in this window; do not substitute a similarly named page or copy fragments from elsewhere into this window's record. If the entry point is not visible, stop the exit process, preserve the known state, and hand it back to the side that maintains those materials to address.

## Window Record

Each time you enter the exit process, first add three lines to this record:

- The exit action that will be taken or has already been taken;
- The last result you can see, and whether that result is still identifiable;
- The exit actions adj-cmake has taken for this window.

"Last visible result" means only the result you can actually see at that moment. Do not backfill it with a later summary, results from another window, or a release conclusion. If the result is empty, its source is unclear, or the same window contains two results whose old/new order cannot be distinguished, leave the record blank. Do not fill in a pass or fail on your own.

## Execution Order

1. **Verify the exit target.**

   First confirm that you are handling the exit window for cmake-quality-signal, not a test or fuzz sample with the same name, or a closeout item for another project. Record the exit action in the window exactly as it is. If the action can only be inferred from a verbal description, or you cannot tell whether it belongs to adj-cmake, stop at this step; do not perform a cleanup action whose purpose is unclear.

2. **Preserve the last visible result.**

   Before the exit action changes the state, confirm that the last visible result will remain available for later review. Record only the state you have already seen. Do not explain why it occurred or use it to declare the release successful. If the result disappears during the operation, preserve the existing record and stop further cleanup; "there should be a result later" cannot replace the evidence you have.

3. **Verify the exit actions for adj-cmake.**

   Review the exit actions that actually took place on the adj-cmake side alongside the first two items. Only confirm whether the actions have been recorded and are still identifiable. Do not attribute actions by the main project or other maintainers to adj-cmake. If you can confirm only the first two items but not this one, the window must not be exited.

4. **Submit the sign-off materials.**

   Once all three items are recorded, hand the window record to the corresponding owner. The owner's sign-off is where release success is determined; this checklist does not sign off on the owner's behalf or treat "exit action executed" as a substitute for sign-off. If you find that the result has changed before sign-off, return to step 2 to update the record, then submit it again.

## Stop Conditions

Stop if any of the following occurs. Do not continue with post-exit cleanup:

- The relationship between the exit action and cmake-quality-signal cannot be confirmed;
- The last visible result is missing, cannot be identified, or does not match the window record;
- The exit actions for adj-cmake have left no record that can be checked;
- The corresponding owner has not yet signed off;
- The state needs to be restored, but the restore action has not yet been validated in a shared environment.

Stopping is not a failure conclusion. When stopping, preserve the window record already written, the visible result, and the action descriptions. Do not delete the original materials to create a seemingly clean window. In particular, do not erase the last result because the release has not yet been signed off; later judgments still need it.

## Handling Deviations

If the exit action has already started and the last visible result subsequently becomes unavailable, stop all further actions immediately. Record what you can confirm and note that the result was not preserved. Do not rerun a similar input to replace the original window's result, or paste in a result from another window.

If you find that the exit actions for adj-cmake do not match the record, first preserve the state that was visible before the change, then stop. An immediate restore is not required here: the restore action has not yet been tried in a shared environment. An unvalidated restore should not be the default operation within the window.

If the owner considers all three items complete but has not yet signed off, the window is still waiting. You may organize the record for the owner's review, but you cannot change the status to release successful. Even after sign-off, it only means that this owner has completed the release judgment; this page still retains the operational trace of the exit window.

## Handoff Checks

Check each item before handoff:

- [ ] Verified this window's materials using `docs/adj-cmake/release/cmake-quality-signal-exit-window-checklist.md`.
- [ ] Recorded the exit action and confirmed that it belongs to the exit window for cmake-quality-signal.
- [ ] Preserved the last visible result, or explicitly recorded that the result was unavailable and stopped.
- [ ] Verified the exit actions for adj-cmake; did not continue the exit when they could not be verified.
- [ ] Handed the three recorded items to the corresponding owner without substituting this checklist for release sign-off.

Do not add speculative causes after the window ends. If a new result appears later or a restore action needs validation, create a separate record and keep it alongside the original three items from this window.

# On-call runbook for dependency boundary failures

## Where to stop first

This page covers a failed run involving `singleheader-supply-boundary`. When on call, first save the original input, the first visible state, the run ID, and the current version of `URLPattern` before deciding whether to continue. The entry point is still `docs/adj-singleheader/runbooks/singleheader-dependency-boundary-audit-failed-run-on-call-page.md`. Do not use a permissions refresh, a restart, or regenerated data in place of the initial observation; if these actions are not themselves steps being validated, taking them makes it impossible to tell where the difference began.

Stop at the current step if any of the following occurs:

- The input before `fragment delimiter` already differs from the most recent known-good sample;
- The state changes after entering `public API`, but the original value has not yet been saved;
- The record does not reach `transactional setter`, or there is no evidence showing whether that setter ran;
- Only the collated results are visible, with no pre-change routing snapshot.

At the stop point, record the object name, the first value that differed, the entry point in use at the time, and any actions already taken. Do not treat "no further errors" as recovery, or mark untested conditions as passing by default.

## Handle differences by branch

### Input and delimiter position differences

Compare only one condition at a time. Do not replace `query delimiter`, `dot segment`, `scheme transition`, and `fragment delimiter` together in the same drill. If a step requires observing `malformed UTF-8`, retain the original input and record that observation separately; do not clean up or convert the encoding first. Write the comparison result back only to the corresponding step; leave other combinations unconfirmed.

If the difference appears at `serialization`, first save the values before and after serialization, then check whether `round trip` ran to completion. Completion does not mean the boundary has been confirmed; proceed to the next step only when you can identify the first object that differs. If `transactional setter` does not appear, stop before the setter and note the missing execution record in the handoff. Do not keep changing the entry point based on guesses.

### Changes to the exit entry point or dependency boundary

Past records include cases where the exit entry point changed versions but the execution records did not cover the change. When reviewing these runs, first retain the pre-change routing snapshot, then check the current entry point. If you confirm that an action points to the old exit action, delete that action following the handling instructions left in AURLD-001; before deletion, save the snapshot and the original action separately, and do not overwrite them with recovery observations afterward. If it has not yet been confirmed whether the action belongs to this run, stop at the difference and do not delete it in advance.

If the difference extends beyond the dependency sources, scope of adoption, and exit responsibilities established around lock and license, or involves maintenance outside this project's scope, do not expand the changes here. Hand off the entry point, observed behavior, original input, and steps already validated to the public interface owner; user communication and this project's own exit criteria stay with this project. All that can be confirmed here is whether the handoff materials are complete.

Local drill results are diagnostic material only and cannot replace a recheck in the public environment. Before the recheck, save the local results and the run version; after the recheck, record the two separately to avoid misreporting a local pass as recovery of the public entry point.

Keep a separate record of interventions. The outstanding items in AURLD-012 require recording who performed the action and when, and must not be combined with recovery observations. If the person, time, or original input is missing, stop at that item; do not fill the gaps with "handled on shift."

Fill in the handoff based on the actual situation:

- Entry-point file and specific step;
- First point of difference, and the original value or snapshot retained;
- Interventions performed, who performed them, and when;
- Hypotheses that were ruled out;
- Current owner of `canonicalization`;
- Time of the next check and branches that remain unverified.

Keep `compatibility matrix`, old entry points, and return actions left by earlier versions as historical material; do not rewrite them as commitments about the current implementation. Preserve the failure state even after service is restored; leave old claims with no new evidence as originally recorded, and do not add a root cause for them.

During the maintenance window, the visible results at the team's public entry point did not match the original plan. versions.body:
# Postmortem on a Public Entry Point Maintenance Discrepancy

This record began with a mismatch during a maintenance window: the team's public entry point had already been included in the maintenance plan, but the results observed at the time did not appear as originally planned. What first became available was not a complete timeline, but a comparison of results. When the entry point's visible state, the maintenance actions that had already taken place, and the expected results were placed side by side, the three did not naturally line up.

The initial draft did not attribute this difference to any individual or to any single maintenance action. What could be confirmed at the time was very limited: an inconsistency occurred during the window; someone first preserved the observed results; temporary recovery was then performed. No single set of materials yet answered where the discrepancy began, who was affected, or whether the old entry point was still in use.

## What Was Preserved at Discovery

The records captured at the time did not begin with a complete account of the background. What they preserved first were the visible results at the entry point and a comparison from before and after recovery. The reason was straightforward: if the entry point was changed back first and the anomaly described afterward, the post-recovery state could easily be mistaken for the state at discovery. The comparison materials were therefore preserved as `serialized before-and-after record`, rather than replaced with a retrospective account.

The conclusions this before-and-after record can support are also limited. It can help identify the visible differences before and after the recovery action, and allow later reviewers to distinguish "what was seen at discovery" from "what was seen after recovery". It cannot establish the actual scope of impact on its own, prove which maintenance action caused the difference, or prove that the old entry point was no longer part of the plan. The initial draft did not contain these conclusions, and later work should not derive nonexistent conclusions from this record.

At the time, checks traced back through the objects and call names in `include/ada/url.h` adjacent to `serialized`, `after`, and `record`. This location only indicates where clues to the before-and-after record were sought at the time. It does not turn a discrepancy in organizational coordination into an attribution to source code, nor does it provide a complete explanation of the public entry point switchover process. This file location is preserved to show the search path taken at the time, not to reduce the incident to a problem in a particular header file.

## What Happened at the Time

- **Initial discovery**: During the maintenance window, the visible results at the public entry point did not match the original plan. The record contains no exact time when the discrepancy began, so the time of discovery cannot be treated as its starting point.
- **Preserving the observed state**: The entry point results and the before-and-after comparison were preserved first. No usage details beyond what was observed were added, and missing context was not filled with speculation.
- **Temporary recovery**: The entry point was temporarily brought back to a state in which work could continue. This action changed the results visible at the time, but did not automatically answer whether the old entry point still existed.
- **Re-examining the records**: The contents from before and after recovery were placed side by side again for comparison. The review confirmed that "the planned outcome did not appear" could only describe the difference at the time, not directly serve as its cause.
- **Preserving the gaps**: The actual impact, the coordination point, the conditions for withdrawing the old entry point, and the steps that produced the discrepancy remained incompletely confirmed.

The relationship between the second and third steps is the easiest part of the timeline to overlook. The observed state was preserved before temporary recovery, so the before-and-after record at least did not completely overwrite the state at discovery with the state after intervention. However, the record itself is not complete enough to reconstruct every maintenance action. It preserves only two facts: the comparison of visible results and that recovery took place.

Recovery also does not mean that everything returned to the original plan. After recovery, the entry point may have become visible again, or may once again have been usable; these are all outcomes of the intervention at the time. They do not mean that all consumers have been confirmed unaffected, still less that the discrepancy cannot recur under the same conditions. The original materials did not preserve the complete scope of usage, so the impact cannot be recorded as having ended simply because the same results were no longer observed after recovery.

## Earlier Assessments in the Initial Draft

The initial draft focused on "the results did not appear as planned". It was reasonable to retain this statement, but it later became easy to read it as "the maintenance plan was not carried out". That reading went beyond the materials available at the time: a mismatch between the visible results and the plan is not enough to confirm that the plan was not carried out, or to confirm how far its execution had progressed.

Another readily offered explanation was that the old entry point had not been withdrawn. This was also unconfirmed. The old entry point might still have been visible, might still have been in use, or the recovery action might simply have preserved some state in which withdrawal remained possible; the existing record cannot distinguish among these possibilities. The fact that this earlier explanation was proposed is preserved here, but it is not elevated to a causal attribution.

The early statement that "the entry point was restored" should therefore also be understood in its original context. It describes the state visible at the time, rather than declaring that the root cause had been fixed. The later review found no materials that could pin the cause on maintenance actions, the entry point switchover, or missing records, so the earlier assessment can only remain a working hypothesis.

This qualification is not intended merely to make the document seem cautious. It directly affects the judgment of later readers: if temporary recovery is recorded as a final fix, an investigation into the same discrepancy next time can easily begin from an already misrepresented starting point; recording the old entry point as withdrawn would also conceal what the recovery action actually preserved.

## Four Control Points Added During Review

The review did not recast the maintenance window as a complete operating procedure, but only added several connections that were clearly missing from the initial draft. They address specific gaps in this discrepancy, rather than prescribing rules for all public entry point maintenance.

**Actual impact.** When recording entry point recovery, distinguish between "the entry point appears to have recovered" and "what impact actual usage experienced". This page contains no verifiable counts, scope, or list of consumers. This gap is preserved, not replaced with the outcome of temporary recovery, and the fact that the same results were no longer observed is not interpreted as zero impact.

**Coordination point.** There needs to be a coordination point that can explain the relationship among the original plan, the maintenance actions, and temporary recovery. The initial draft did not preserve this mapping, and the later review did not add a name, role, or explicit handoff. This page can therefore only identify the gap: the records captured at the time do not establish who was to confirm whether the plan and recovery aligned.

**Old entry point that can be withdrawn.** Temporary recovery cannot be recorded simply as "recovery succeeded". It is still necessary to know whether the old entry point remains in use, whether it can be withdrawn, and which part of the plan its withdrawal would affect. The current record does not contain these results. Marking the old entry point as something that can be withdrawn does not mean that withdrawal has already occurred; it only prevents later investigations from conflating "temporary recovery" with "the old entry point has been dealt with".

**Before-and-after record.** `serialized before-and-after record` should be preserved as material captured at the time. It is used to compare visible states before and after maintenance and help identify where the state changed; it is not a substitute for impact assessment, nor does it demonstrate closure on the root cause. Gaps in the before-and-after record remain, especially the actions before the discrepancy first appeared and the state of the old entry point after recovery.

The four control points also cannot substitute for one another. Even confirming that the old entry point can be withdrawn does not establish the actual scope of impact; even finding the coordination point does not establish when the discrepancy began; even if the before-and-after record shows that the entry point became visible again, it does not prove that every part of the maintenance plan was completed as originally intended. The problem with the initial draft was precisely that it compressed these different levels into the single statement "the results did not line up".

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    window[Maintenance window] --> mismatch[Visible results do not match the original plan]
    mismatch --> record[Preserve before-and-after records]
    record --> restore[Temporary recovery]
    restore --> review[Review again]
    review --> unknown[Impact, coordination point, old entry point, and starting point remain unconfirmed]
```

The sequence in the diagram describes only the traces of the response preserved in this record. It does not provide a causal chain for the discrepancy, nor does it depict "Review again" as meaning that the cause has been confirmed. The maintenance window, the mismatch in results, the before-and-after record, and temporary recovery have a chronological order; the materials remain insufficient to establish which action caused the difference.

## The Limits of Recovery

The value of temporary recovery lies in returning the public entry point to a state in which work can continue, avoiding continued exposure of the same obvious discrepancy during the window. Its limits are equally clear: recovery changes the entry point results visible at the time, not the impact that has already occurred or the maintenance process that remains unconfirmed.

This distinction must be preserved in the postmortem, because "recovery" can easily acquire additional meanings in different reading contexts. For those handling the situation, it is a response action; for impact assessment, it is only a point in time; for root-cause analysis, it carries no evidentiary weight. Without materials establishing the discrepancy's starting point, the old entry point's state, and the actual impact, describing recovery as a complete fix would mislead later readers into thinking that the investigation had ended.

The original record also contains no evidence that the discrepancy existed only before recovery. The absence of the same visible results after recovery only indicates that the subsequent record did not preserve the same phenomenon; it cannot substitute for confirmation of usage. This limitation is retained here because this page is still used as reference material for the earlier window, not because it covers all subsequent entry point maintenance scenarios.

## Relationship to the On-Call Record

DOC-47 preserves the on-call cheat sheet and can serve as a guide to the entry points for that shift. It should not be used to fill in the scope of impact, coordination relationships, or root cause that this postmortem did not record. The two sets of materials have different focuses: this page preserves one discrepancy, temporary recovery, and the gaps remaining after review; the on-call record is only suitable for carrying forward the operational pointers that needed to be remembered at the time.

This distinction also explains why this page was not expanded into new maintenance instructions. It records an inconsistency within one window and the limits on conclusions that remained afterward. Directly backfilling later operating habits would make it difficult for readers to distinguish facts that had already occurred at the time from practices that developed later.

## Unanswered Questions

- What state was the entry point actually in when the discrepancy first appeared?
- Between the original plan and the visible results, what is missing: a maintenance action, an entry point switchover, or the record itself?
- After temporary recovery, could the old entry point still be safely withdrawn?
- Who can confirm the actual impact, rather than merely confirm that the entry point is visible again?
- Which segment is still missing from the before-and-after record that would allow the observed difference to be separated from its cause?

These questions were not answered in this review. They do not invalidate the discovery, preservation, and temporary recovery that took place, but only indicate that this postmortem preserves a discrepancy and traces of the response during one maintenance window. The earlier description of the recovery results still has reference value, but it cannot be treated as the current authoritative account of public entry point maintenance.

# Public Entry Point Maintenance FAQ

### What does the existing pattern-canon entry point prove?

The entry point is still there, which shows that the team has brought the candidate path under shared maintenance. Maintainers can take this to mean that the relevant compatibility behavior has been exercised; if someone reports the same issue later, return to this entry point first rather than splitting off another parallel path.

### Who is responsible for withdrawing the candidate path?

The people who maintain the public entry point handle it. Since the candidate path was included in the entry point, its withdrawal should also be completed as part of changes to the entry point; the person who proposed the candidate doesn't need to keep a separate withdrawal note.

### Under what conditions can it be closed?

It can be closed once the entry point opens normally and the relevant results can be found in the review. If adjacent behavior changes later, log it as a new issue.

# Shared Entry Point Maintenance FAQ

The old answers have not been taken down, because some people still use them to find the shared entry point. But their claim that "the entry point exists" means validation is complete came across as too strong during review. The original answers and follow-up notes are included together below, so we don't leave only a fragment of the later conclusion.

### What can the existing pattern-canon entry point prove?

The old answer was: if the entry point is still there, that means the candidate path has been brought under shared maintenance, and the relevant compatibility behavior has also been exercised. That judgment conflated entry-point visibility with test results. At most, the entry point shows that the discussion did not introduce a separate set of names; it cannot replace a rerun for that compatibility item, nor does it show that adjacent behavior is unchanged.

### Who is responsible for withdrawing the candidate path?

The old answer assigned withdrawal to whoever maintains the shared entry point and assumed that the person who proposed the candidate did not need to leave a separate note. The review did not find anyone explicitly assigned to handle withdrawal. If the candidate path is to be withdrawn, the entry-point maintainer can propose a change, but who actually carries it out and who confirms that the old path is no longer being used remain unanswered questions. We cannot infer that withdrawal is complete just because the candidate name no longer appears in the entry point.

### Under what conditions can an item be closed?

The earlier criteria were simply that the entry point could be opened and the result could be found in the review. This would make items without a focused rerun look complete. The working rule added later was: Close a compatibility item only after the focused regression and adjacent unchanged behavior pass from a clean checkout, the result is linked to review, and any release or incident claim is tied to its dated event window.

Items without a focused compatibility test run can therefore be logged, but we cannot answer that they "can already be closed"; whether closure is justified remains unknown. DOC-50 contains notes from a single-variable rerun; that record cannot be stretched into proof that the candidate path has been withdrawn or that all adjacent behavior has passed. The old entry-point answers can still be used to find people and names, but should no longer be used as a basis for closure.

# Public Entry Point Single-Variable Rerun

Reviewing the records left by the first two rounds, first separate an old conclusion. `include/ada/url_search_params.h` is the file location fixed when searching along search-params at the time; it makes it possible to return to that comparison, but cannot be used to conclude that the public entry point permanently belongs at this location. The first round tied the path and entry point too closely. This old wording remains above so later reviews do not mistake the location method used at the time for confirmed ownership.

This rerun uses only three things together: the fixed repository state, the entry point reached from the call name, and one release or incident artifact adjacent to the rerun period. The first two are for comparison; the third only indicates what period that round took place in. It cannot fill in the call relationship or provide an impact scope for entry-point maintenance. Keeping all three in one place prevents the path, call name, and time-related material from each carrying a judgment beyond its original purpose.

Operational constraints are unchanged. In each round, keep the repository state and call entry point fixed first, then replace only one input under verification; do not adjust the remaining conditions along the way. The old entry point is also not deleted for now, because we need to know whether it can still be rolled back, rather than treat it as the only entry point that remains usable. If the entry point and input are changed at the same time, a change in landing point cannot be attributed to either condition, and the first two rounds can no longer be compared with each other.

The first visible branch is still where the call entry point lands. If the landing point matches the fixed state, record which input was replaced in this round and confirm whether the old entry point is retained; if it does not, record only the difference and first fill the coordinator information into the blank field. Earlier records did not quantify the actual impact, and the coordinator field did not contain a name. These two gaps remain and should not be filled using path lookup or adjacent release or incident material.

Another easy-to-confuse point is that finding search-params only shows that the search passed through the object in the fixed state; it is not itself evidence of "public entry-point maintenance succeeded." The latter judgment still requires checking whether the call entry point actually landed on the same object in that round. The old version connected these two actions into a single signal; now they are checked in sequence: identify the comparison object first, then inspect where the call entry point lands. This preserves the original rerun sequence without elevating the file location into interface ownership.

No third run was performed after recording the first fork. The first two rounds were not compiled into a final summary either; they retain only their respective input changes, landing-point determinations, and old-entry status. The adjacent release or incident artifact likewise remains only a time marker and was not used to explain why a particular call changed. This limitation is why the old notes can still be cited, and also why they are not currently suitable to serve directly as an entry-point maintenance conclusion.

If work continues, next time change only another value of the same input under verification, while keeping the repository state and call entry point fixed. First check whether the landing point crosses the first fork; if it does not, do not expand further to the impact scope. If it does, then fill in the coordinator and add the rollback record for the old entry. The ownership of the file location will not be resolved in this rerun.
